label: Make It Work 3D
title: Turning a Plastic Bottle into a Rocket #shorts
desc:
What would it take to turn a plastic bottle into a spacecraft? One problem, one fix at a time.
A thought experiment. A real plastic bottle cannot go to space.

The science:
- Fins keep a rocket pointed straight by using the airflow.
- As you climb, the outside air thins. In space, the air inside pushes outward with about 1 atmosphere of pressure.
- In space, the sunlit side gets very hot and the shaded side very cold. Apollo spacecraft rotated slowly to spread the heat (the "barbecue roll").
- Solar panels make no power in Earth's shadow, so spacecraft store energy in batteries.
- On the way back, the air in front of the spacecraft is strongly compressed and gets extremely hot. A heat shield protects it, and parachutes slow it down.

Voice: Kokoro TTS (Apache-2.0)
Music: YouTube Audio Library
Map data: Natural Earth (public domain)

lines.say: Let's turn a plastic bottle into a rocket!
Step one: a rocket engine on the bottom.
Launch!
Uh oh. It starts spinning.
Add fins, and it flies straight.
Higher up, the air gets thin, and the bottle swells.
Metal bands hold it together.
We made it to space. But the sunny side is roasting.
Wrap it in insulation.
Now we can't see outside.
Add a window.
The sun shines through the window. One side is still hot.
So, spin it slowly on purpose, to spread the heat.
The spinning that was a problem, is now the fix.
No electricity.
Unfold the solar panels.
In Earth's shadow, everything goes dark.
Charge a battery while the sun is out.
Coming home, the air in front gets squeezed, and extremely hot.
A heat shield on the bottom.
Still falling too fast.
Open the parachute.
Splashdown. It's a plastic bottle, so it floats!
